title: Putting two words together
keyIdea: Two words say more than one. 'Milk' names a thing, but 'more milk' says what you want, and 'all gone' says there is none left. Two words can say who is doing something (dog run), whose a thing is (Daddy shoe), where it is (teddy bed) or what it is like (big ball). Both words must fit what is happening. When a child says two words, the grown-up says them back a bit longer ('Yes, the dog is running!'), and the child copies the next words.
familyTip: At snack time, pause before you give more. If your child says 'more', wait a moment, then say 'More apple?' and give it when they try two words. When they say two words, say them back with one or two more, warmly, and never ask them to say it again properly.

visual.caption: One word or two words? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: join two word cards to ask and tell, say who does what, drag things to their owners, pick where a toy is, and say it back a bit longer.

kid: One word is good. Milk! But two words say more. More milk! Now Mum knows you want more.
Is your plate empty? Say: all gone! Is the car going? Wave and say: bye car!
Two words can say who and what. The dog runs: dog run! The baby sleeps: baby sleep!
Two words can say whose it is, and where it is. Daddy shoe! Teddy bed! Pick two words that fit what you see.
adult: Ages 2 to 3. Most children say at least two words together, like 'more milk', by about 2 years (CDC milestones, 2022). Development Matters (2021) links this stage to talking with an adult every day. Key words: two-word phrase, word combination, expansion, recast.

Early two-word phrases carry a small set of meanings (Brown, 1973): more (more juice), all gone, no and bye; who does an action (dog run); whose a thing is (Daddy shoe); where it is (teddy bed); and what it is like (big ball). The little words such as 'is', 'the' and 'in' come later, so 'teddy bed' is a real step forward, not a mistake to fix.

Common mistakes by grown-ups: asking the child to repeat a full sentence, which can stop the talk; answering with no words, so there is nothing new to copy; and replying with a long sentence that is too far ahead. Be careful to say their words back with one or two more ('Teddy is in bed!'). Studies of this recast step show it helps children learn new words and grammar (Cleave and colleagues, 2015). Children slip too: one word when two would say more, a word that does not fit the picture, and words the wrong way round, such as 'milk more'.

In the lab your child joins two word cards to ask and tell, says who does what, drags a shoe, a sock and a hat to their owners, and picks where a toy is. Then you choose what to say back. Each wrong choice gets its own reply that names the slip.

practice.prompt: The cup is empty. Which says the most?
practice.hint: Which one says what you want, and fits the cup?
practice.explain: More milk uses two words: more says you want some again, and milk says what.

practice.prompt: You have {n} blocks. You say "more block" and get 1 more. How many blocks now?
practice.hint: Count the blocks you have, then count 1 more.
practice.explain: {n} blocks and 1 more make {=n+1} blocks. Saying more block asked for one more.

practice.prompt: The dog is running. Which two words fit?
practice.hint: Who is in the picture? What is it doing?
practice.explain: Dog says who, and run says what it does. Both words fit the picture.

practice.prompt: {n} cars go by. You say "bye car" to each one. How many times do you say it?
practice.hint: One wave for each car. Count the cars.
practice.explain: One bye car for each car, so you say it {n} times.

practice.prompt: Your child says "car go". What is the best thing to say back?
choices: No. Say: the car is going.
practice.hint: Which reply keeps the talk going and gives new words to copy?
practice.explain: Say their words back a bit longer. They hear the next words without being told they were wrong.

pool.prompt: The plate is empty. Which two words fit?
pool.hint: What do we say when there is none left?
pool.explain: All gone says there is nothing left. Gone on its own is just one word.

pool.prompt: Baby has one sock on. Here is the other sock. Whose is it?
pool.hint: Who has one sock on already?
pool.explain: Baby sock says whose it is. Baby has the other sock on.

pool.prompt: Teddy is in the box. Which two words fit?
pool.hint: Look where teddy is. Is it the bed or the box?
pool.explain: Teddy box says where teddy is. Teddy bed does not fit, because teddy is in the box.

pool.prompt: You put {n} ducks in the bath and say "duck bath" for each. Then 1 more duck. How many ducks in the bath?
pool.hint: Count the ducks in the bath, then 1 more.
pool.explain: {n} ducks and 1 more make {=n+1} ducks in the bath.

pool.prompt: Your child says "big ball". Which reply helps most?
choices: A big ball! Kick the big ball.
That ball rolled all the way under the sofa in the other room last night.
pool.hint: Which reply is just a bit longer than big ball?
pool.explain: A big ball, kick the big ball adds one or two words. A long sentence is too far ahead to copy.

pool.prompt: Mia says "milk more". What was her slip?
choices: The words are the wrong way round
pool.hint: Which word do grown-ups say first: more or milk?
pool.explain: We say more milk, with more first. Say it back the right way round: more milk!

pool.prompt: You say "more grape" {n} times, and each time you get 1 grape. How many grapes do you get?
pool.hint: One grape each time you ask. Count how many times you asked.
pool.explain: One grape for each "more grape", so {n} asks get {n} grapes.

pool.prompt: The bird is flying. Which two words fit?
pool.hint: Say who first, then what it does.
pool.explain: Bird fly says who, then what it does. Fish fly does not fit, and fly bird is the wrong way round.
